cases.title: Case Study 1
cases.facts:
On the evening of November 14, 2024, Arjun Singhania, a software
engineer, returned to his Mumbai apartment unexpectedly early from a
business trip. Upon entering his bedroom, he discovered his wife, Priya,
in a compromising position with his close friend and business partner,
Rohan. Shocked and enraged, Arjun began yelling. Rohan, rather than
showing remorse, mocked Arjun, stating, "You were always too busy for her
anyway." A heated argument ensued. Arjun, in a fit of rage, grabbed a
heavy brass lamp from the bedside table and struck Rohan repeatedly on
the head. Rohan collapsed and died on the spot from severe craniocerebral
trauma. Arjun immediately called the police and confessed. He was charged
with murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
cases.issues:
- Did Arjun's actions constitute murder under Section 300 of the IPC,
punishable under Section 302?
- Did the discovery of his wife's infidelity, coupled with the victim's
mocking words, constitute "grave and sudden provocation" to attract
Exception 1 to Section 300?
- Can the charge be mitigated to culpable homicide not amounting to
murder, punishable under Section 304 Part I of the IPC?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The Prosecution argued that Arjun committed premeditated, brutal murder.
They contended that striking an unarmed man multiple times on the head
with a heavy brass lamp demonstrates a clear intention to cause death, or
at least bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to
cause death (Section 300, Thirdly). The State relied on the landmark
K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra, arguing that for provocation to
be a defense, the loss of self-control must be absolute and immediate.
They argued that because Arjun had the presence of mind to grab a
specific weapon and strike multiple times, he had not lost his senses
entirely, and the retaliation was disproportionate to the provocation of
mere words from Rohan.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Defense)
The Defense argued for the application of Exception 1 to Section 300 IPC.
They contended that catching a spouse in flagrante delicto is
universally recognized as the highest form of grave and sudden
provocation. The defense argued that Rohan's cruel taunts served as a
supervening provocation that entirely stripped Arjun of his power of
self-control. Relying on Muthu v. State of Tamil Nadu, the defense
asserted that there was no premeditation, no prior enmity regarding the
affair (as Arjun was unaware), and the act was committed in the heat of
passion before there was time for the blood to cool. Therefore, the
offense falls strictly under Section 304 Part I.
cases.judgment:
The Sessions Court convicted Arjun under Section 304 Part I of the IPC
(Culpable homicide not amounting to murder), rejecting the murder charge
under Section 302. The Defense partially prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court reasoned that the visual shock of adultery, immediately
compounded by the victim's insolent and taunting words, met the threshold
for "grave and sudden provocation." The judge noted that the human mind
is not a machine that can perfectly calibrate a response in a state of
sheer emotional trauma. The weapon used (a bedside lamp) was an object of
opportunity, further proving the lack of premeditation. The Court applied
the "reasonable man test," concluding that a reasonable person from
Arjun's social background, thrust into that sudden, humiliating, and
agonizing scenario, could foreseeably lose their power of self-control.
However, because he had the intention to cause fatal injury in that
moment of passion, he was guilty under Section 304 Part I, not Part II.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Doctrine of Grave and Sudden Provocation
under Exception 1 to Section 300 of the IPC. It establishes that
verbal taunts immediately following a shocking discovery (like adultery)
can collectively constitute adequate provocation. It also highlights the
crucial distinction between intention formed in a cool state of mind
(murder) versus intention formed while deprived of self-control (culpable
homicide).

cases.title: State of Karnataka v. Vikram Datta
cases.facts:
Vikram Datta, a wealthy jeweler in Bengaluru, had been receiving
extortion threats from a local gang. On the night of August 5, 2024,
three masked men broke into his isolated farmhouse. Vikram, awakened by
the shattered glass, grabbed his licensed 9mm pistol. As he stood at the
top of his stairs, he saw the men in the living room below, armed with
iron rods. Vikram shouted a warning. One intruder yelled, "Kill him and
take the keys!" and took a step toward the staircase. Vikram immediately
fired five shots. Two shots hit the advancing intruder in the chest,
killing him. The other two intruders turned and fled toward the door.
Vikram fired two more shots at the fleeing men, hitting one in the back
and paralyzing him. Vikram was charged with murder and attempted murder.
cases.issues:
- Was Vikram Datta legally justified in causing the death of the first
intruder under the Right of Private Defense of body and property
(Sections 96 to 106 IPC)?
- Did Vikram exceed his right of private defense by shooting the fleeing
intruder in the back, thereby becoming an aggressor?
- Does the apprehension of danger continue when the assailants are in
retreat?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The Prosecution conceded that the initial break-in justified some level
of self-defense. However, they argued that Vikram's response was grossly
disproportionate and vindictive. Under Section 99 of the IPC, the right
of private defense does not extend to inflicting more harm than
necessary. The State argued that shooting the first intruder five times
was excessive. More importantly, shooting the fleeing intruders in the
back was a clear act of retaliation, not defense. Relying on State of
U.P. v. Ram Swarup, the State argued that the right of private defense
extinguishes the moment the apprehension of danger to the body ceases.
Fleeing men pose no imminent threat.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Defense)
The Defense relied on Sections 100 and 103 of the IPC. They argued that
an armed home invasion at night accompanied by a verbal threat to life
creates a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, justifying
lethal force. Regarding the fleeing intruders, the defense argued that in
the darkness and chaos of a home invasion, a homeowner experiencing
extreme adrenaline and terror cannot be expected to "weigh his response
in golden scales" (Darshan Singh v. State of Punjab). Vikram had a
split-second to react and ensure the threat was neutralized, fearing they
might take cover and return fire.
cases.judgment:
The High Court acquitted Vikram for the death of the first intruder but
convicted him of causing grievous hurt under Section 326 of the IPC for
shooting the fleeing intruder. The State partially prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court bifurcated the incident. For the first intruder, the Court held
Vikram acted within his rights under Section 100 and 103 IPC. The
intruders were armed, broke in at night, and expressed homicidal intent.
Lethal force was justified. However, regarding the shots fired at the
retreating men, the Court strictly applied Section 102 IPC: the right of
private defense of the body commences as soon as a reasonable
apprehension of danger arises and continues only as long as such
apprehension continues. When the intruders turned their backs and fled,
the immediate threat evaporated. Shooting them in the back was punitive,
not defensive. Therefore, Vikram exceeded his right of private defense.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case delineates the strict boundaries of the Right of Private
Defense. It establishes the principle of Continuing Apprehension of
Danger, affirming that self-defense is a protective right, not a
punitive one. Once the aggressor retreats and the imminent threat ceases,
any further use of force transforms the defender into an aggressor under
Indian criminal jurisprudence.

cases.title: State of Kerala v. Dr. Thomas Kurian
cases.facts:
Dr. Thomas Kurian, a brilliant but reclusive mathematician, had a
documented history of paranoid schizophrenia, though he had stopped
taking his medication six months prior. On October 10, 2024, Dr. Kurian
attacked his neighbor, Mr. Iyer, unprovoked, in the community park. He
stabbed Mr. Iyer multiple times with a kitchen knife, shouting that Mr.
Iyer was a "reptilian spy transmitting radioactive signals" into his
brain. Dr. Kurian then sat calmly on a bench until the police arrived. He
did not resist arrest but asked the officers if they had "secured the
alien transmitter." He was charged with attempted murder under Section
307 IPC.
cases.issues:
- Is Dr. Kurian entitled to the general exception of unsoundness of mind
under Section 84 of the IPC?
- At the time of committing the act, was the accused, by reason of
unsoundness of mind, incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that
what he was doing was either wrong or contrary to law?
- What is the evidentiary burden required to establish legal insanity
versus medical insanity?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The Prosecution argued that while Dr. Kurian suffered from medical
insanity (schizophrenia), he did not meet the strict threshold of legal
insanity required by Section 84 IPC, which is based on the McNaughten
Rules. The State pointed out that Dr. Kurian used a deadly weapon, aimed
for vital organs, and waited for the police, indicating he knew the
nature of the physical act he was committing (stabbing a human). The
Prosecution relied on Surendra Mishra v. State of Jharkhand, arguing
that mere eccentric behavior or psychiatric illness does not grant
absolute immunity if the cognitive faculties to distinguish right from
wrong remain intact.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Defense)
The Defense argued that Dr. Kurian was suffering from a severe psychotic
delusion that fundamentally severed his connection to reality. They
presented psychiatric testimony proving that his disease created a
terrifying alternate reality where his life was in imminent danger from
non-human entities. Under Section 84, even if a person knows the physical
nature of the act, they are protected if they do not know it is wrong.
Because Dr. Kurian genuinely believed he was acting in self-defense
against a "reptilian spy," he lacked the mens rea (guilty mind)
required for a criminal offense.
cases.judgment:
The Sessions Court acquitted Dr. Thomas Kurian by reason of unsoundness
of mind under Section 84 IPC, and ordered his secure confinement in a
psychiatric facility under Section 335 of the CrPC. The Defense
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The judge provided a nuanced analysis of Section 84. The Court
acknowledged the distinction between medical and legal insanity but ruled
that Dr. Kurian's specific delusion satisfied the legal test. The
critical factor was his cognitive incapability to understand that his act
was "wrong." In Dr. Kurian's diseased mind, Mr. Iyer was not a human
neighbor but a lethal alien threat. Therefore, while he knew he was
striking something, he did not understand the legal or moral wrongness
of striking a human being, because his mind had replaced reality with a
profound, terrifying hallucination. The total absence of motive and his
bizarre post-incident behavior corroborated the complete collapse of his
rational faculties.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case clarifies the application of Section 84 IPC (Unsoundness of
Mind). It reinforces that the critical test is the cognitive capacity
at the exact moment of the offense. It establishes that a profound,
documented psychotic delusion that genuinely prevents the accused from
understanding the moral or legal wrongfulness of an act satisfies the
criteria for legal insanity, thereby negating mens rea.

cases.title: State of Gujarat v. Apex Petrochemicals Ltd.
cases.facts:
Apex Petrochemicals Ltd. operated a large chemical plant in Surat. To cut
operational costs, the Board of Directors approved a measure to bypass a
critical automated safety valve on a high-pressure reactor, despite
warnings from the Chief Safety Officer that this violated standard
operating procedures. On May 12, 2024, the reactor over-pressurized and
exploded, releasing a toxic cloud that killed 15 factory workers and
severely injured 50 nearby residents. The State prosecuted not only the
plant manager but also the corporation itself, Apex Petrochemicals Ltd.,
along with its Managing Director, for Culpable Homicide not amounting to
murder (Section 304 Part II IPC).
cases.issues:
- Can a fictitious legal entity like a corporation possess the requisite
mens rea (knowledge or intention) to be charged with an offense like
culpable homicide?
- Should the doctrine of "Alter Ego" (Identification Doctrine) be applied
to attribute the criminal intent of the directors to the corporation?
- Can a corporation be charged with an offense for which the mandatory
punishment includes imprisonment?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The Prosecution, relying on the Supreme Court's landmark judgment in
Iridium India Telecom Ltd. v. Motorola Incorporated, argued that
corporations can no longer claim immunity from criminal prosecution for
offenses requiring mens rea. The State utilized the "Alter Ego"
doctrine, arguing that the Board of Directors was the "directing mind and
will" of the company. Since the Board consciously chose to bypass safety
protocols with the knowledge that it was likely to cause death
(satisfying Section 304 Part II), that knowledge must be attributed to
the company itself. The State demanded massive fines and the piercing of
the corporate veil to imprison the directors.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Defense)
The Defense argued that a corporation, having no physical body or mind,
cannot be imprisoned or form the mens rea required for bodily offenses
like culpable homicide. They relied on traditional jurisprudence, arguing
that corporate liability should be restricted to statutory offenses with
strict liability or those punishable only by fines. They argued that
charging the company with Section 304 Part II is a legal impossibility
because the statute mandates imprisonment. The defense also argued that
the negligence of the plant manager cannot automatically be elevated to
the "knowledge" of the corporate entity.
cases.judgment:
The High Court upheld the charges against both the Managing Director and
Apex Petrochemicals Ltd. under Section 304 Part II. The company was
ordered to pay unprecedented fines, and the directors faced trial for
imprisonment. The State prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court decisively rejected the archaic notion that corporations are
immune from mens rea offenses. Applying the "Identification Doctrine,"
the judge ruled that when the individuals who constitute the "directing
mind" of a company act within their scope of authority, their actions and
their guilty minds are the actions and minds of the company. Because
the Board deliberately compromised safety for profit, knowing the lethal
risks, the company itself possessed the mens rea for culpable homicide.
Regarding the punishment paradox (imprisonment for a corporation), the
Court followed the precedent set in Standard Chartered Bank v.
Directorate of Enforcement, holding that where a statute mandates
imprisonment and fine, a corporate offender can be punished with the
fine alone, while the human directors face imprisonment.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case cements the doctrine of Corporate Criminal Liability in
India for severe mens rea offenses. It fully integrates the Alter Ego
/ Identification Doctrine into bodily offenses, proving that companies
can be tried for culpable homicide. It resolves the jurisdictional hurdle
by affirming that courts can bifurcate mandatory punishments, levying
fines on the corporation while imprisoning its directing humans.

cases.title: State of Delhi v. Kunal Verma
cases.facts:
Kunal Verma, an IT professional, was rejected by his colleague, Neha.
Seeking revenge, Kunal scraped hundreds of normal photographs of Neha
from her public social media profiles. He used advanced open-source AI
tools to superimpose Neha's face onto highly explicit pornographic videos
(deepfakes). He then created anonymous accounts and distributed these
videos to Neha's family, colleagues, and employer, tagging them with
defamatory captions. Neha suffered severe psychological trauma and was
forced to resign. Kunal was traced via his IP address and charged under
Section 67 and 67A of the Information Technology (IT) Act, Section 354D
(Stalking) of the IPC, and Section 499/500 (Defamation) of the IPC.
cases.issues:
- Do digitally manipulated synthetic media (deepfakes) constitute the
publishing of "sexually explicit acts" under Section 67A of the IT Act,
even if the victim's actual body is not in the video?
- Does the act of monitoring a woman's public social media to harvest
photos for malicious use constitute "stalking" under Section 354D of the
IPC?
- Is there a conflict between the specific provisions of the IT Act and
the general provisions of the IPC (Defamation) in cyberspace?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The Prosecution argued for maximum sentencing, noting the devastating
impact of deepfakes on a woman's dignity. They argued that Section 67A of
the IT Act (publishing material containing sexually explicit acts)
applies fully because the perception and harm caused are identical to
real revenge porn. The digital face makes the identity undeniable to the
viewer. For stalking (Section 354D), the State argued that Kunal's
systematic harvesting of her digital footprint to terrorize her
constituted "monitoring her use of the internet" with an intent to foster
fear and distress.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Defense)
The Defense argued for a narrow, literal interpretation of the penal
statutes. They contended that Section 67A requires the material to depict
the person in explicit acts. Since the body belonged to an anonymous
pornographic actor and only the face was digitally altered, Neha was not
actually depicted participating in the act. Therefore, Section 67A is
legally inapplicable. They also argued that viewing publicly available
photos on Instagram does not meet the legal definition of "stalking" or
"monitoring," as Neha willingly broadcasted those images to the public.
cases.judgment:
The Cyber Appellate Tribunal and subsequently the Delhi High Court
convicted Kunal on all counts, sentencing him to rigorous imprisonment
under Section 67A of the IT Act and Section 354D of the IPC. The State
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court took a progressive, purposive approach to statutory
interpretation in the digital age. The judge scoffed at the defense's
literal interpretation of Section 67A. The Court ruled that the essence
of the crime is the non-consensual violation of a woman's sexual privacy
and dignity. If the synthetic media is designed to make viewers believe
the victim is engaged in explicit acts, it squarely falls under Section
67A. The technology used is irrelevant; the intent and effect are
paramount. Regarding stalking, the Court held that while looking at
public profiles is not inherently illegal, the systematic, obsessive
harvesting of those images to weaponize them against the victim
transforms innocent browsing into malicious "monitoring," strictly
satisfying the ingredients of Section 354D.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This is a landmark precedent for Cyber Jurisprudence and Deepfakes.
It expands the interpretation of Section 67A of the IT Act to
explicitly encompass synthetic media and deepfakes, ensuring that
technological loopholes do not defeat the law's intent. It also
modernizes the definition of Digital Stalking (Section 354D IPC),
confirming that weaponizing a person's public digital footprint
constitutes criminal monitoring.

cases.title: State of UP v. Rahul Tiwari
cases.facts:
Rahul Tiwari and Sneha were in a consensual sexual relationship for three
years. Rahul had repeatedly promised to marry Sneha, and their families
had even met. Based entirely on this solemn promise, Sneha consented to
physical intimacy. However, it was later discovered that months before
making these promises to Sneha, Rahul had already legally married another
woman in his hometown and kept it a secret to maintain his relationship
with Sneha. When Sneha discovered the truth, she filed a criminal
complaint. Rahul was charged with rape under Section 375 of the IPC, on
the grounds that her consent was vitiated by a "misconception of fact"
under Section 90 of the IPC.
cases.issues:
- Does a false promise of marriage constitute a "misconception of fact"
under Section 90 of the IPC, thereby vitiating a woman's consent to
sexual intercourse?
- What is the legal distinction between a mere breach of promise (which
is not rape) and a false promise made with the intent to deceive from the
inception?
- Did Rahul's actions fulfill the criteria for rape under Section 375 of
the IPC?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The Prosecution argued that Sneha's consent was entirely conditional upon
the belief that she and Rahul were to be married. Relying on the Supreme
Court's ruling in Anurag Soni v. State of Chhattisgarh, the State
argued that Rahul had no intention of marrying Sneha from the very
beginning, as evidenced by his pre-existing, concealed marriage. This was
not a case of a relationship simply falling apart; it was a calculated
fraud. Because the consent was obtained through deceit and a fundamental
misconception of fact (his marital status and intent), the consent is
legally void under Section 90 IPC, rendering the physical relationship
rape under Section 375.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Defense)
The Defense argued that criminalizing consensual relationships due to
broken promises is a dangerous overreach of the law. They cited Pramod
Suryabhan Pawar v. State of Maharashtra, arguing that Sneha was an
educated, independent adult who consented to a sexual relationship over a
prolonged period. A breach of a promise to marry, even if morally wrong,
does not retrospectively criminalize years of consensual intimacy. The
defense contended that proving "intent to deceive from the inception" is
nearly impossible and that Section 90 should be applied to fundamental
misunderstandings of the physical act itself, not future matrimonial
commitments.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court of India upheld the High Court's conviction of Rahul
Tiwari for rape under Section 376 of the IPC. The State prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court carefully distinguished between a "breach of promise"
and a "false promise." The Court noted that in many relationships,
partners may genuinely intend to marry but later separate due to
unforeseen circumstances; this does not constitute rape. However, Rahul's
case was unequivocally different. The indisputable fact that he was
already married when he promised marriage to Sneha proved that his
promise was a calculated, fraudulent lie from day one. He extracted her
consent through active deception. The Court ruled that under Section 90
IPC, consent given under a misconception of fact is no consent at all if
the man knows that the consent was given in consequence of such
deception. Therefore, the act squarely fell within the definition of
rape.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case solidifies the jurisprudence surrounding Consent and
Misconception of Fact (Section 90 IPC). It establishes a clear, bright-
line rule: a false promise of marriage made in bad faith from the very
inception vitiates consent. It protects individuals from sexual
exploitation achieved through calculated, fraudulent matrimonial deceit,
distinguishing it from ordinary relationship failures.

cases.title: State of Punjab v. Harpreet Singh
cases.facts:
Harpreet Singh, a fiery student leader, organized a massive rally
protesting a newly enacted, highly controversial agricultural reform law.
During the rally, Harpreet gave a passionate speech condemning the
Central Government, calling them "blood-sucking tyrants" and urging the
massive crowd to "paralyze the capital until the government begs for
mercy." Following the speech, a splinter group from the rally attacked a
local government office, burning it down and injuring police officers.
The police arrested Harpreet, charging him with Sedition (Section 124A
IPC) and Criminal Conspiracy (Section 120B IPC) to wage war against the
state, arguing his speech directly incited the violence.
cases.issues:
- Does robust, aggressive criticism of the government and calls for mass
disruption amount to "Sedition" under Section 124A of the IPC?
- Where is the legal line drawn between the fundamental right to free
speech (Article 19(1)(a)) and the incitement of violence?
- Can Harpreet be held liable for Criminal Conspiracy (Section 120B) for
the violence committed by the splinter group without proof of an explicit
agreement?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The Prosecution argued that Harpreet's speech was not mere dissent; it
was a calculated attempt to excite disaffection, hatred, and contempt
against the lawfully established government. They argued that words like
"paralyze the capital" were direct dog-whistles for violent insurrection.
Relying on the proximity of the speech to the actual burning of the
government office, the State argued the mens rea for conspiracy was
evident. The State contended that as the organizer and primary speaker,
Harpreet implicitly conspired with the crowd, creating the combustible
environment that led directly to the violent acts.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Defense)
The Defense vigorously invoked the landmark judgment of Kedar Nath Singh
v. State of Bihar. They argued that Section 124A must be strictly
construed to protect democratic dissent. Criticizing the government, even
using strong, hyperbolic language, is a constitutional right. Sedition
only applies if the speech directly incites imminent public disorder or
violence. The defense argued Harpreet's speech was political hyperbole,
and he never explicitly called for arson or attacks on police.
Furthermore, they argued that criminal conspiracy requires a "meeting of
the minds"-a specific agreement to commit an illegal act. A speaker
cannot be held liable for the independent, spontaneous criminal acts of a
rogue splinter group.
cases.judgment:
The High Court quashed the charges of Sedition (Section 124A) and
Criminal Conspiracy (Section 120B) against Harpreet Singh, ordering his
immediate release. The Defense prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a robust defense of free speech. Applying the Kedar
Nath principles, the judge ruled that citizens have a right to say or
write whatever they like about the government, provided they do not
incite people to violence. The Court found Harpreet's speech, though
militant and aggressive, fell short of incitement to imminent lawless
action. "Paralyzing the capital" in the context of a protest usually
implies strikes and blockades, not necessarily arson. Regarding
conspiracy, the Court held that Section 120B requires concrete proof of
an agreement between two or more persons to commit an offense. Guilt by
association or mere presence at a rally is insufficient. The State failed
to prove Harpreet coordinated or agreed to the attack on the government
office.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case vigorously reinforces the Constitutional Safeguards against
Sedition. It establishes the Incitement to Violence Test,
clarifying that strong political dissent, hyperbole, and calls for civil
disobedience do not constitute sedition unless there is a clear,
proximate incitement to public disorder. It also strictly defines the
evidentiary requirements for Criminal Conspiracy, rejecting guilt by
mere association in mass protests.

cases.title: State of West Bengal v. Rajat Bose
cases.facts:
Rajat Bose was the Chief Financial Officer (CFO) of a prominent Kolkata-
based charitable trust that provided funds for pediatric cancer
treatments. Over three years, Rajat manipulated the accounting software.
He diverted small fractions of incoming donations-amounts so small they
initially evaded audit detection-into a complex web of shell companies
owned by his brother-in-law. Rajat accumulated ₹12 Crores before a
whistleblower exposed the scheme. The State charged Rajat with Criminal
Breach of Trust by a public servant/clerk/servant (Section 408/409 IPC)
and Cheating (Section 420 IPC). Rajat argued it was a civil dispute
regarding accounting errors and unauthorized loans, not a criminal
matter.
cases.issues:
- What are the essential ingredients required to constitute the offense
of "Criminal Breach of Trust" under Section 405 of the IPC?
- Does the diversion of funds entrusted to a corporate officer into
personal shell companies constitute "dishonest misappropriation"?
- Can a single act constitute both Criminal Breach of Trust and Cheating?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The Prosecution argued that this was a textbook case of Criminal Breach
of Trust. They demonstrated that the Trust legally "entrusted" its funds
to Rajat in his capacity as CFO (establishing dominion over property).
Instead of executing his fiduciary duty, Rajat acted with dishonest
intention to misappropriate and convert those funds for his own use via
his brother-in-law's shell companies. The State relied on S.W.
Palanitkar v. State of Bihar, arguing that the clandestine nature of the
diversion proved the mens rea. They also pressed the Cheating charge,
arguing he deceived the donors and the board.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Defense)
The Defense attempted to muddy the waters, claiming the funds were
temporarily moved as high-yield short-term investments meant to generate
more money for the charity, and that the inability to repay was a civil
breach of contract. They argued that to prove Section 405, the state must
prove an absolute conversion of the property. Furthermore, the defense
argued that charging Rajat with both Cheating and Breach of Trust is
legally contradictory. Cheating requires deception from the very
beginning to obtain property, while Breach of Trust requires lawful
obtainment (entrustment) followed by later misappropriation.
cases.judgment:
The Sessions Court convicted Rajat Bose of Criminal Breach of Trust under
Section 409 IPC and sentenced him to 10 years rigorous imprisonment.
However, the Court acquitted him of the Cheating charge under Section
420. The State partially prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court dismantled the defense's "civil dispute" argument. The judge
ruled that the transfer of charitable funds to undisclosed, related-party
shell companies without board approval is the epitome of dishonest
misappropriation. The fact that the money was taken establishes the
offense of Criminal Breach of Trust; whether he intended to put it back
later (which the court doubted) is legally irrelevant once the initial
misappropriation is complete. However, the Court agreed with the defense
regarding the mutually exclusive nature of the charges in this specific
factual matrix. Since Rajat was lawfully entrusted with the funds by
virtue of his employment, he did not acquire them through initial
deception. Therefore, he cannot be convicted of cheating, but he is fully
liable for breaching the trust placed in him.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case clearly delineates the boundaries of White-Collar Crime,
specifically Criminal Breach of Trust (Section 405 IPC). It clarifies
that temporary misappropriation or the intent to restore the property
later does not negate the criminal offense. Furthermore, it establishes
the crucial jurisprudential distinction between Cheating (deception at
inception) and Breach of Trust (lawful entrustment followed by
dishonest conversion).

cases.title: State of Rajasthan v. Om Prakash
cases.facts:
Om Prakash owned a prominent dairy distribution network. A surprise
inspection by food safety officers intercepted a massive tanker of milk
belonging to his company. Laboratory tests confirmed the milk was heavily
adulterated with detergent and synthetic urea, posing a severe health
hazard. Om Prakash was entirely unaware of this; it was later proven that
the truck driver and a local farm manager had conspired to water down the
milk and add chemicals to maintain its density to make a side profit.
Nonetheless, the State charged Om Prakash, as the owner, under the
Prevention of Food Adulteration Act (PFA Act) and Section 272 of the IPC
(Adulteration of food intended for sale).
cases.issues:
Is mens rea (guilty mind) an essential ingredient for offenses under
public health and safety statutes like the Prevention of Food
Adulteration Act?
- Can a business owner be held criminally liable for the acts of their
employees under the doctrine of Strict Liability in criminal law?
- Does the absence of knowledge regarding the adulteration provide a
valid legal defense for the proprietor?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The Prosecution argued that public health statutes operate on the
principle of Strict Liability. Relying on the English precedent of
Alphacell Ltd v. Woodward and Indian cases dealing with food
adulteration, the State argued that the legislature deliberately omitted
words like "knowingly" or "intentionally" from the PFA Act. The mere
physical act (actus reus) of storing or distributing adulterated food
for sale is sufficient for a conviction. The State contended that if
owners could escape liability by simply claiming ignorance and blaming
low-level employees, the entire regulatory framework protecting public
health would collapse.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Defense)
The Defense grounded its argument in the fundamental maxim of criminal
law: actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea (an act does not make a
person guilty unless the mind is also guilty). They argued that Om
Prakash was a victim of his employees' fraud. He had implemented standard
quality checks at the processing plant, and the adulteration occurred in
transit. Punishing a man with imprisonment for an act he had no knowledge
of, and did not intend to commit, violates the basic tenets of justice
and Article 21 of the Constitution.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court upheld Om Prakash's conviction under the special
legislation (PFA Act) but quashed the IPC charges. The State partially
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court provided a masterclass on the displacement of mens
rea. The Court ruled that while mens rea is a foundational rule, the
legislature holds the sovereign power to create absolute or strict
liability offenses, particularly concerning public welfare, health, and
safety. In statutes dealing with food adulteration, the overriding public
interest requires that the distributor ensures absolute purity at their
peril. Therefore, under the PFA Act, Om Prakash's lack of knowledge is
utterly irrelevant; he is strictly liable as the owner. However, the
Court noted that Section 272 of the general Indian Penal Code explicitly
requires the act to be done "knowing" or having "reason to believe" the
food is adulterated. Since the prosecution proved strict liability but
failed to prove actual knowledge, the IPC charge could not stand.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case highlights the Exception to the Mens Rea Rule. It firmly
establishes the doctrine of Strict Criminal Liability in Statutory
Offenses, particularly in public welfare legislation. It signifies that
for crimes endangering mass public health, the burden of absolute
compliance rests on the business owner, and the defense of ignorance or
employee sabotage is legally void.

cases.title: State of Assam v. David Zeliang
cases.facts:
David Zeliang, a 22-year-old college student, was in a romantic
relationship with Maya, who was 17 years and 10 months old. Maya's
parents strongly opposed the relationship and restricted her from leaving
the house. Desperate, Maya called David, begging him to take her away so
they could get married, threatening self-harm if he refused. David drove
to her house at midnight; Maya willingly packed her bags, climbed out the
window, and drove away with him to a neighboring state. Maya's father
filed an FIR. David was arrested and charged with Kidnapping from lawful
guardianship under Section 361 of the IPC, punishable under Section 363.
cases.issues:
- Does taking a minor girl away with her active, enthusiastic consent
constitute the offense of "Kidnapping from lawful guardianship" under
Section 361 IPC?
- Does the fact that the minor initiated the escape and threatened self-
harm absolve the accused of the charge?
- Whose consent is legally material under Section 361-the minor's or the
lawful guardian's?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The Prosecution argued a strict, literal interpretation of Section 361
IPC. The law states that whoever "takes or entices" any minor (under 18
for females) out of the keeping of their lawful guardian without the
consent of such guardian commits kidnapping. The State relied on the
landmark Supreme Court judgment in S. Varadarajan v. State of Madras.
They argued that Maya's consent is entirely immaterial in the eyes of the
law because a minor is legally incapable of giving valid consent to leave
her guardian's custody. By physically driving her away, David actively
participated in the "taking," thereby completing the offense.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Defense)
The Defense argued that David did not "take or entice" Maya; rather, she
abandoned her guardian's keeping entirely on her own volition. They
heavily relied on the nuances of the same Varadarajan case. In that
precedent, the Court noted a distinction between a man soliciting a girl
to leave, and a girl completely severing her ties with her family,
walking up to a man, and asking for his protection. The defense argued
Maya was the active agent; she threatened self-harm to force David's
hand. David merely facilitated her independent decision, which should not
be criminalized as kidnapping, especially considering she was only weeks
away from turning 18.
cases.judgment:
The High Court convicted David Zeliang under Section 363 IPC for
kidnapping. The State prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly applied the parameters of Section 361. The judge
emphasized that the object of the statute is to protect the sacred right
of the lawful guardian, not just the minor. Therefore, the minor's
consent, eagerness, or even initiation of the plan is legally irrelevant
if she is under 18. While acknowledging the defense's reference to
Varadarajan, the Court distinguished the facts. In Varadarajan, the
girl had already left the house and met the accused on the street. In the
present case, David drove his car to her house at midnight to facilitate
her exit. This active physical assistance in removing her from the
physical boundaries of the guardian's domain constitutes "taking" in law.
Her threat of self-harm, while mitigating for sentencing, does not alter
the physical completion of the crime.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case rigidly enforces the legal definition of Kidnapping from
Lawful Guardianship (Section 361 IPC). It establishes the absolute
legal principle that a minor's consent is entirely immaterial in
cases of kidnapping. It clarifies that any active physical facilitation
by the accused to remove a minor from the guardian's control constitutes
"taking," strictly protecting the custodial rights of the parents until
the stroke of midnight on the child's 18th birthday.

cases.title: State of Madhya Pradesh v. Rameshwar & Ors.
cases.facts:
On the evening of June 12, 2024, Rameshwar and four of his associates
went to the agricultural fields of the victim, Brijesh, to settle a long-
standing property dispute. The group was armed with lathis (wooden
sticks) with the pre-discussed plan to give Brijesh a "severe beating" to
scare him off the land. An altercation ensued. Unexpectedly, amidst the
scuffle, Rameshwar pulled a concealed country-made pistol from his
waistband and shot Brijesh in the chest, killing him instantly. The other
four associates immediately dropped their lathis and fled the scene in
panic. All five men were subsequently arrested and charged with Murder
under Section 302 read with Section 149 (Unlawful Assembly) and Section
34 (Common Intention) of the IPC.
cases.issues:
- Can the four associates be held vicariously liable for the murder
committed by Rameshwar under Section 34 or Section 149 of the IPC?
- Did the common intention of the group extend to causing death, or was
it limited only to causing grievous hurt?
- Does the sudden, independent act of one member of an unlawful assembly
make all members liable for the aggravated offense?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The Prosecution argued that all five accused formed an unlawful assembly
with a common object to use criminal force. Relying on Section 149, they
argued that since the murder was committed in prosecution of the common
object of the assembly, or was such that the members knew it was likely
to be committed, all are equally liable for murder. Alternatively, under
Section 34, the State argued that carrying lethal weapons (even if
concealed by one) implies a pre-arranged plan to use lethal force if
necessary. The presence of the associates emboldened Rameshwar to pull
the trigger.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Defense)
The Defense for the four associates argued that there was absolutely no
"meeting of the minds" regarding the use of a firearm or causing death.
They cited Mahbub Shah v. Emperor, emphasizing that "common intention"
requires a pre-arranged plan and prior concert. The associates only
agreed to use lathis to cause hurt; they had no knowledge Rameshwar
possessed a gun. When he fired the shot, it was his independent,
individual act that exceeded the scope of their shared intention. Their
immediate flight demonstrated their lack of complicity in the murder.
cases.judgment:
The Sessions Court convicted Rameshwar of Murder under Section 302 IPC.
The four associates were acquitted of Murder but convicted of voluntarily
causing hurt under Section 323 IPC. The Defense for the associates
partially prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court meticulously dissected the doctrines of vicarious liability.
The judge noted that for Section 34 to apply, the criminal act must be
done in furtherance of the common intention of all. The evidence proved
the common intention was solely to beat the victim with sticks. The use
of the firearm was a sudden, unilateral escalation by Rameshwar.
Regarding Section 149, the Court ruled that murder was not the common
object of the assembly, nor was it a natural or probable consequence of
an agreement to commit assault with sticks that the other members should
have anticipated. Punishing the associates for a murder they did not
plan, foresee, or assist in would violate the foundational principles of
criminal culpability.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes critical boundaries for Vicarious Liability under
Sections 34 and 149 of the IPC. It reinforces the legal principle that
a sudden, independent escalation by one accused that fundamentally
alters the nature of the crime cannot automatically be attributed to co-
accused unless active participation or prior knowledge of the lethal
intent is proven beyond a reasonable doubt.

cases.title: State of Haryana v. Sunita Devi's In-Laws
cases.facts:
Sunita Devi married Rajesh in February 2022. On October 15, 2024 (within
three years of marriage), Sunita was admitted to a hospital with 80% burn
injuries and succumbed to them two days later. Prior to her death, her
parents had filed multiple police complaints alleging that Rajesh and his
parents subjected Sunita to immense physical and mental cruelty,
demanding a luxury car as additional dowry. The defense claimed Sunita
accidentally caught fire while cooking on a faulty kerosene stove. The
dying declaration recorded by the magistrate was ambiguous, with Sunita
stating, "The stove burst, they were fighting with me about the car
again." Rajesh and his parents were charged under Section 304B (Dowry
Death) and Section 498A (Cruelty) of the IPC.
cases.issues:
- Are the ingredients of Section 304B (Dowry Death) strictly fulfilled,
warranting the invocation of the legal presumption against the accused?
- Does the ambiguity in the dying declaration regarding the exact nature
of the fire (accidental vs. homicidal/suicidal) negate the charge of
dowry death?
- Does the presumption under Section 113B of the Indian Evidence Act
shift the entire burden of proof to the accused?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The Prosecution heavily relied on the statutory presumption under Section
113B of the Evidence Act. They argued that all prerequisites of Section
304B were met: the death occurred within seven years of marriage, it was
caused by burns (unnatural circumstances), and it was proven via prior
police complaints that Sunita was subjected to cruelty by her husband and
in-laws "soon before her death" in connection with a demand for dowry.
Once these facts are established, the State argued, the court shall
presume that the accused caused the dowry death, rendering the ambiguity
of the dying declaration less critical.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Defense)
The Defense argued that the primary cause of death was a pure accident,
as suggested by the first half of the dying declaration ("The stove
burst"). They cited Kamesh Panjiyar v. State of Bihar, arguing that
Section 304B is a severe penal provision and must be strictly construed.
If the death is an accident, the chain of causation is broken, regardless
of prior domestic disputes. They argued the prosecution failed to prove
that the cruelty "soon before death" was the direct proximate cause
driving her to suicide or resulting in homicide.
cases.judgment:
The High Court convicted Rajesh and his parents under Section 304B and
Section 498A of the IPC, sentencing them to life imprisonment. The State
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a powerful ruling on the legislative intent behind
Section 304B. The judge noted that the statute was specifically drafted
to combat the "silent crime" behind closed doors where direct evidence is
rarely available. The Court held that the prosecution successfully
established the foundational facts: unnatural death, within 7 years, and
cruelty related to dowry. Once established, Section 113B of the Evidence
Act mandates a statutory presumption of guilt. The burden entirely
shifted to the defense to prove the death was a pure, unrelated accident.
Given the history of abuse and the dying declaration indicating an
argument over dowry at the very moment of the fire, the defense failed to
rebut the presumption. The Court ruled that whether the death was
suicidal or homicidal is irrelevant under 304B, so long as it is
unnatural and preceded by dowry-related cruelty.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case aggressively enforces the Statutory Presumption of Dowry
Death (Section 113B of Evidence Act). It solidifies the legal principle
that under Section 304B IPC, the prosecution need not prove whether
the death was a murder or suicide; they must only prove unnatural death
preceded by dowry cruelty, shifting the burden of innocence entirely onto
the accused.

cases.title: State of Kerala v. Dr. Akash Nair
cases.facts:
Dr. Akash Nair, a senior abdominal surgeon, performed a routine
appendectomy on a 25-year-old patient, Rahul. During the surgery, a power
outage caused a brief failure of the backup generator, creating chaos in
the operating theater. In the rush to close the incision before the
patient's anesthesia compromised, Dr. Nair left a surgical sponge inside
Rahul's abdominal cavity. He also failed to conduct the standard post-
operative sponge count. Three weeks later, Rahul developed severe
septicemia due to the rotting sponge and died. Dr. Nair was charged with
Culpable Homicide not amounting to murder (Section 304 Part II IPC) and
alternatively, Causing death by negligence (Section 304A IPC).
cases.issues:
- Does leaving a surgical instrument inside a patient constitute "gross
negligence" sufficient to attract criminal liability under Section 304A
of the IPC?
Did the doctor possess the requisite mens rea (knowledge that his act
is likely to cause death) to be charged with Culpable Homicide under
Section 304 Part II?
- What is the threshold distinguishing civil medical malpractice from
criminal medical negligence?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The Prosecution argued that Dr. Nair's actions went beyond mere human
error and amounted to gross, criminal negligence. Leaving a sponge inside
a patient and failing to conduct a mandatory post-operative inventory
count is a blatant dereliction of duty. They argued that a surgeon of his
seniority possesses the knowledge that leaving a foreign object in the
abdomen is highly likely to cause fatal infection, thereby justifying the
harsher charge of Section 304 Part II.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Defense)
The Defense heavily relied on the Supreme Court guidelines established in
Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab. They argued that doctors are protected
from criminal prosecution unless their negligence is of such a high
degree that it exhibits a total disregard for the patient's life. The
defense highlighted the extenuating circumstance of the sudden blackout,
arguing it was an error in judgment made during a crisis, not a reckless
or willful act. They argued that while this may constitute civil
liability (tort), it lacks the mens rea for criminal liability, let
alone Culpable Homicide.
cases.judgment:
The Court acquitted Dr. Nair of Culpable Homicide (Section 304 Part II)
but convicted him of Causing death by negligence (Section 304A IPC). The
State partially prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
Applying the Jacob Mathew test, the Court clarified the boundary
between civil and criminal negligence in the medical profession. To
convict a doctor criminally, the negligence must be "gross"-meaning the
doctor did something no competent medical professional would do under the
same circumstances. The Court reasoned that while the blackout created
panic, the failure to perform a basic sponge count post-surgery is a
fundamental breach of standard medical protocol, crossing the threshold
into gross negligence (Section 304A). However, the Court rejected the
Culpable Homicide charge. Section 304 Part II requires subjective
knowledge that the act is likely to cause death. Dr. Nair did not
know he left the sponge; he was negligently unaware. Therefore, the
higher mens rea requirement was absent.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the Jacob Mathew Guidelines for Criminal Medical
Negligence. It establishes the critical distinction between Section
304A (Gross Negligence without Intent) and Section 304 Part II
(Knowledge of Likelihood of Death), affirming that professional
incompetence, even if fatal, must exhibit "gross recklessness" to warrant
criminal sanctions, protecting medical professionals from malicious
prosecution for simple errors.

cases.title: CBI v. Nirav Kothari
cases.facts:
Nirav Kothari, a deputy manager at a prominent public sector bank,
colluded with a diamond merchant. Without entering the transactions into
the bank's core banking software (CBS), Nirav used his authorized SWIFT
terminal credentials to issue fraudulent Letters of Undertaking (LoUs)
worth ₹5,000 crores to overseas branches of other Indian banks. These
overseas branches released funds to the merchant based on the bank's
guarantee. When the merchant defaulted, the bank was held liable. Nirav
was charged under Section 409 (Criminal breach of trust by a public
servant), Section 420 (Cheating), and Section 468 (Forgery for purpose of
cheating) of the IPC, read with the Information Technology Act.
cases.issues:
Can an employee who uses their own valid, authorized credentials to
issue unauthorized guarantees be charged with "Forgery" under Section
463/464 of the IPC?
- Does bypassing internal accounting software while executing a legally
binding external electronic transmission constitute making a "false
electronic record"?
- Is a public sector bank employee considered a "public servant" for the
purpose of aggravated breach of trust under Section 409?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (CBI)
The Prosecution argued that Nirav's actions constitute textbook forgery
in the digital age. Under Section 464 (Making a false document/electronic
record), creating an electronic record with the intent to deceive
constitutes forgery. Even though Nirav used his own passwords, he
generated SWIFT messages claiming the bank had authorized the LoUs and
held collateral, which was a material falsehood. The CBI further argued
that as an employee of a nationalized bank, Nirav is a "public servant"
entrusted with dominion over the bank's credit, and his actions willfully
defrauded the public exchequer (Section 409).

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Defense)
The Defense argued a highly technical interpretation of Forgery. They
cited Mir Nagvi Askari v. CBI, arguing that for a document to be
forged, it must be executed claiming to be made by someone else. Since
Nirav used his own SWIFT ID and had the authority to issue LoUs, the
documents were "genuine documents containing false statements," not
"forged documents." Making a false statement is not forgery. They argued
he might be liable for cheating, but not forgery.
cases.judgment:
The Special CBI Court convicted Nirav Kothari on all counts, including
Section 468 (Forgery) and Section 409 (Breach of Trust). The Plaintiff
(CBI) prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court forcefully updated the interpretation of forgery for the
digital banking era. The judge ruled that the defense's reliance on
archaic definitions of forgery failed to account for electronic records.
Under the IT Act read with Section 464 IPC, a person makes a false
electronic record if they transmit it intending it to be believed that it
was authorized by a person (the Bank's Board/CBS system) by whom they
knew it was not authorized. By willfully bypassing the CBS, Nirav
stripped the transactions of their legitimate corporate authorization,
rendering the SWIFT messages false electronic records created to defraud.
Furthermore, the Court affirmed that employees of nationalized banks are
public servants, and utilizing the bank's global credit lines for
private, unrecorded gain represents the highest degree of criminal breach
of trust.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This judgment sets a massive precedent for Cyber-Financial Fraud and
Electronic Forgery. It clarifies that authorized access does not
preclude forgery; if authorized credentials are used to generate
unrecorded, unauthorized electronic guarantees designed to deceive the
global banking system, it strictly constitutes making a "false electronic
record" under Section 464 IPC.

cases.title: State of UP v. Brijesh & Gang
cases.facts:
Brijesh and five other armed men intercepted a luxury passenger bus on a
deserted highway at 2:00 AM. They boarded the bus, terrorized the
passengers with firearms, and looted cash and jewelry. The operation took
twenty minutes. As the gang disembarked and began running toward their
getaway vehicles parked 100 meters away, a passenger named Suresh pulled
out a licensed revolver and fired at them. Brijesh turned around and
fired a burst from his assault rifle, killing Suresh instantly, before
the gang escaped. All six were caught and charged under Section 396 of
the IPC (Dacoity with Murder).
cases.issues:
Does a murder committed while retreating after the loot has been
secured fall under the ambit of "murder committed in so committing a
dacoity" (Section 396)?
- Does the act of the victim (Suresh) firing first break the causal
chain, turning the murder into an act of private defense by the dacoits?
- Are all six gang members liable for the death penalty/life imprisonment
under Section 396, even if only one fired the fatal shot?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The State argued that the transaction of dacoity is not complete the
moment the property is snatched. Relying on Shyam Behari v. State of
UP, the prosecution asserted that the act of escaping safely with the
looted property is an integral, contiguous part of the commission of
dacoity. Therefore, murder committed to facilitate an escape is murder
committed "in so committing dacoity." Consequently, under the strict
vicarious liability imposed by Section 396, if any one of the five or
more persons commits murder during this transaction, every single
member is equally liable for the maximum punishment.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Defense)
The Defense argued that the primary offense of robbery/dacoity had
concluded. The men had left the bus and were 100 meters away. The
transaction was over. They cited older precedents suggesting that once
the loot is secure and the robbers are in retreat, any subsequent
violence is a separate offense. Furthermore, they argued that since
Suresh fired first, Brijesh acted in self-defense. Most importantly, the
defense for the other five members argued it is grossly unjust to hold
them liable for a spontaneous shooting committed by one person while they
were running away.
cases.judgment:
The High Court convicted all six accused under Section 396 IPC (Dacoity
with Murder). The State prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court definitively rejected the defense's timeline of the crime. The
judge ruled that the offense of dacoity is a continuing transaction. It
begins with the attempt to rob, continues through the actual looting, and
extends to the immediate flight and carrying away of the stolen property.
Since Brijesh fired to secure their escape with the loot, the murder was
inextricably linked to the dacoity. The Court dismissed the "self-
defense" argument, noting that an aggressor committing a violent felony
has no right of private defense against a victim attempting to stop them.
Most crucially, the Court affirmed the draconian nature of Section 396.
Unlike Section 34 (Common Intention), Section 396 does not require proof
that murder was part of the pre-planned intention; the mere fact that a
murder occurs during the transaction of dacoity renders all co-dacoits
absolutely and vicariously liable.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case cements the Doctrine of Continuing Transaction in Dacoity.
It enforces the absolute Vicarious Liability under Section 396 IPC,
establishing the severe legal principle that all participants in a
dacoity are equally liable for a murder committed by any one member
during the looting or the immediate getaway, irrespective of prior
intention to kill.

cases.title: State of Punjab v. Simranjit Kaur
cases.facts:
Simranjit Kaur was a senior manager at a corporate firm. Over a period of
eight months, she systematically targeted a junior employee, Aman. She
publicly ridiculed his work, called him "worthless," denied his leave
applications for his mother's surgery, and threatened him with
termination daily. Aman fell into deep depression. On Monday morning,
Aman jumped from the office terrace, leaving a suicide note stating:
"Simranjit Kaur has made my life a living hell. She is the sole reason I
am ending my life. I cannot take her torture anymore." Simranjit was
charged with Abetment of Suicide under Section 306 of the IPC.
cases.issues:
- Do workplace harassment, severe reprimands, and verbal abuse constitute
"instigation" as defined under Section 107 of the IPC?
- Is a suicide note naming a specific individual sufficient to fulfill
the mens rea requirement for abetment of suicide?
- What is the threshold distinguishing a strict, demanding boss from a
criminal abettor?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The Prosecution argued that Simranjit's continuous, targeted
psychological torment was designed to break Aman's spirit. They argued
that "instigation" under Section 107 does not require an explicit command
like "go die." A continuous course of conduct that creates a situation so
unbearable that the victim has no alternate option but to commit suicide
qualifies as instigation. The suicide note, written immediately prior to
death, serves as a powerful dying declaration establishing the direct
proximate link between her harassment and his death.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Defense)
The Defense strongly relied on Supreme Court precedents like Madan Mohan
Singh v. State of Gujarat and Sanju @ Sanjay Singh Sengar v. State of
MP. They argued that to attract Section 306, there must be a clear mens
rea-an active, intentional aiding or instigating of the suicide. Being a
harsh, demanding, or even toxic manager does not translate to a criminal
intent to drive someone to death. The defense argued that Aman may have
been hypersensitive, and holding superiors criminally liable for employee
suicides would paralyze corporate administration and disciplinary
mechanisms.
cases.judgment:
The High Court quashed the criminal proceedings against Simranjit Kaur,
acquitting her of charges under Section 306 IPC. The Defense prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a legally sound, albeit morally complex, judgment.
The judge heavily emphasized that abetment involves a mental process of
instigating a person or intentionally aiding a person in doing a thing.
Without a positive act on the part of the accused to instigate or aid in
committing suicide, conviction cannot be sustained. The Court ruled that
mere harassment, workplace pressure, or verbal abuse-however
reprehensible-does not legally amount to "instigation" unless there is a
clear mens rea to push the victim to suicide. The Court noted that an
individual's threshold to handle stress varies; criminal law cannot be
applied based solely on the hypersensitivity of the victim. While
Simranjit's behavior was callous and toxic, the prosecution failed to
prove she intended for Aman to kill himself.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case strictly delineates the boundaries of Abetment of Suicide
(Section 306 IPC) in professional settings. It establishes the legal
principle that workplace harassment or toxic management does not
automatically constitute abetment without explicit proof of mens rea-
a deliberate, active intention to push the victim to end their life.

cases.title: State of Maharashtra v. Sameer Desai
cases.facts:
Sameer Desai planned to murder his business rival, Tariq. He purchased
what he believed was a lethal dose of arsenic from the dark web. He
invited Tariq to a reconciliation dinner and poured the powder into
Tariq's coffee. Tariq drank it but suffered no ill effects. Police later
intercepted Desai's communications, uncovered the plot, and arrested him.
Forensic analysis of the powder revealed it was completely harmless
powdered sugar; Desai had been scammed by the online seller. Sameer was
charged with Attempt to Murder under Section 307 of the IPC.
cases.issues:
- Can a person be convicted of attempting to commit a crime if the
completion of the crime was factually impossible?
Does pouring sugar into a drink fulfill the actus reus (guilty act)
required for an attempt to murder?
- How does Indian penal jurisprudence treat the doctrine of "Factual
Impossibility"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The Prosecution argued that the essence of criminal attempt lies in the
intent combined with an overt act toward the commission of the offense.
Sameer had the absolute mens rea (intent to kill) and performed the
final actus reus necessary on his part (poisoning the drink). Relying
on the illustrations provided in Section 511 of the IPC (attempting to
steal from an empty pocket), the State argued that Indian law does not
recognize factual impossibility as a defense. Sameer did everything in
his power to commit murder; his failure was due to circumstances entirely
beyond his control, not a lack of intent or effort.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Defense)
The Defense argued a highly technical interpretation of Section 307. The
section penalizes acts done "under such circumstances, that if he by that
act caused death, he would be guilty of murder." The defense argued that
pouring sugar into a cup is not an act "under such circumstances" that
could ever cause death. Because the substance was entirely harmless,
the act itself was innocuous. They argued that criminalizing harmless
acts based purely on malicious thoughts verges on prosecuting "thought
crimes," and the act must have at least some proximate capacity to
achieve the intended result.
cases.judgment:
The Sessions Court convicted Sameer Desai of Attempt to Murder under
Section 307 of the IPC. The State prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court decisively rejected the defense of factual impossibility. The
judge reasoned that the focus of attempt liability is the culpability of
the actor, not the physical mechanics of the outcome. The Court held that
Section 307 must be read in conjunction with the broader principles of
Section 511 (punishment for attempting to commit offenses). The Indian
Penal Code explicitly criminalizes attempts where the crime is impossible
(e.g., shooting at a shadow believing it to be a person, or picking an
empty pocket). Sameer's intention to kill was resolute, and his action
(administering what he believed was poison) was the final step required
to execute that intention. The fact that the means chosen were factually
inadequate due to third-party deception does not absolve his criminal
culpability.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case firmly embeds the rejection of the Doctrine of Factual
Impossibility in Indian criminal jurisprudence. It establishes the
legal principle that if a person forms a requisite criminal intent and
performs an overt act toward its execution, they are guilty of an
Attempt (Section 307/511 IPC), even if the completion of the crime
was physically impossible due to factors unknown to the accused.

cases.title: State of TN v. Karthi & The Daily Chronicle
cases.facts:
Karthi, an investigative journalist for The Daily Chronicle, published
a front-page exposé alleging that a sitting Cabinet Minister was involved
in a massive real estate scam. The article was based on a leaked,
unverified whistleblower dossier. The article explicitly called the
Minister "corrupt," a "fraudster," and a "thief of public lands." The
Minister immediately filed a criminal defamation suit under Section
499/500 of the IPC, claiming the documents were forged and his reputation
was irreparably destroyed. Karthi pleaded the exceptions under Section
499, claiming he acted in "good faith" for the "public good."
cases.issues:
- Does the publication of unverified, defamatory allegations against a
public official based on leaked documents fall under the protection of
the First Exception (Truth for Public Good) or the Ninth Exception
(Imputation made in Good Faith) of Section 499 IPC?
- What constitutes "due care and attention" (good faith) for an
investigative journalist under Indian criminal law?
- How is the balance struck between freedom of the press (Article
19(1)(a)) and the right to reputation (Article 21) in criminal
defamation?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Minister)
The Minister (Complainant) argued that press freedom is not a license to
assassinate character. He pointed out that Karthi did not independently
verify the leaked dossier, nor did he ask the Minister for a comment
prior to publication. Relying on Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India,
he argued that the right to reputation is an integral part of the Right
to Life under Article 21. By publishing highly damaging accusations
without basic journalistic verification, Karthi acted with sheer
recklessness, stripping him of the "good faith" defense under the Ninth
Exception.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Defense)
The Defense championed Article 19(1)(a), arguing that journalists play a
crucial role in exposing corruption. They relied on the Ninth Exception
to Section 499, which protects imputations made in good faith for the
protection of public interests. They argued Karthi received the dossier
from a highly placed, historically reliable source. Given the urgency of
the real estate auction mentioned in the dossier, he published it to
alert the public. Demanding absolute, proven truth before publication
would create a chilling effect, paralyzing investigative journalism
against powerful politicians.
cases.judgment:
The Magistrate Court convicted Karthi of Criminal Defamation under
Section 500 IPC, sentencing him to simple imprisonment and a fine. The
Complainant prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court struck a delicate balance, ultimately prioritizing reputation
over reckless publication. The judge noted that the First Exception
(Truth) was unavailable because Karthi could not prove the dossier was
factually true. Therefore, the case hinged on the Ninth Exception (Good
Faith). Under Section 52 of the IPC, "good faith" requires "due care and
attention." The Court ruled that standard journalistic ethics-cross-
checking documents, seeking corroboration, and contacting the subject for
a rebuttal-constitute "due care." Karthi skipped all these steps in a
rush to break the story. The Court held that publishing severe,
unverified allegations based solely on an anonymous leak is an act of
gross negligence, not good faith. The press has a duty to the public, but
that duty requires verifying facts, not amplifying unverified slander.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case defines the strict parameters of Good Faith (Section 52
IPC) in the context of Criminal Defamation (Section 499 IPC). It
establishes that the defense of "public good" requires investigative
journalists to demonstrate rigorous "due care and attention"
(verification and seeking comment) prior to publication, ensuring press
freedom does not devolve into unprotected character assassination.

cases.title: State of Gujarat v. Aman Patel
cases.facts:
Aman Patel owned a drone equipped with a high-resolution camera. He
frequently flew it over his residential neighborhood. One afternoon, he
deliberately hovered the drone outside the third-floor apartment window
of his neighbor, Kavita, while she was changing clothes in her bedroom.
The window was slightly open, and Kavita had an expectation of privacy.
Kavita noticed the drone, panicked, and reported it to the police. The
police seized the drone and recovered the video files. Aman was charged
under Section 354C (Voyeurism) and Section 354 (Assault or criminal force
to woman with intent to outrage her modesty) of the IPC.
cases.issues:
- Can flying a drone outside a window satisfy the ingredients of
"Assault" or "Criminal Force" required to attract Section 354 IPC?
- Does Section 354C (Voyeurism) apply when the recording is done via a
remote-controlled device rather than direct physical proximity?
- Does a woman have a legal expectation of privacy in her home if her
window is partially open to the outside world?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The Prosecution argued that Aman's conduct was a blatant violation of
Kavita's sexual privacy. Regarding Section 354C (Voyeurism), the State
argued the law is technology-neutral: capturing an image of a woman
engaging in a private act where she has an expectation of privacy
fulfills the offense, regardless of whether a camera phone or a drone is
used. The State also pressed Section 354, arguing that intentionally
flying a noisy drone up to a woman's bedroom window constitutes an
"assault"-an intentional act that creates an apprehension of criminal
force, designed specifically to outrage her modesty and deeply shock her
sense of decency.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Defense)
The Defense conceded the drone flight but challenged the applicability of
the statutes. For Section 354, they argued that "assault" and "criminal
force" require physical proximity or a gesture indicating immediate
physical violence (Sections 350/351 IPC). A drone hovering outside cannot
physically assault someone. For Section 354C, they argued that because
the window was partially open to a public airspace, Kavita lost her
absolute expectation of privacy.
cases.judgment:
The Court acquitted Aman of Section 354 (Outraging Modesty) but convicted
him under Section 354C (Voyeurism) of the IPC. The State partially
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a modern interpretation of privacy laws. The judge
dismissed the Section 354 charge, agreeing with a strict interpretation
of the IPC: Section 354 requires physical "assault" or "criminal force."
Merely looking, or filming remotely, lacks the physical components of
assault defined in the code. However, the Court came down heavily on the
Voyeurism charge (Section 354C). The judge scoffed at the defense's "open
window" argument. A person changing in their bedroom inherently possesses
a reasonable expectation of privacy. The law protects a woman from being
watched in private spaces, and employing a drone to bypass physical
boundaries demonstrates deliberate, predatory intent. The mode of
capturing the image is legally immaterial; the violation of privacy is
the core offense.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case clarifies the distinct boundaries between physical and visual
sexual offenses. It establishes that remote, digital surveillance of
private acts strictly falls under Section 354C (Voyeurism), affirming
that the law is technology-neutral. It also clarifies that Section 354
(Outraging Modesty) strictly requires the elements of physical assault
or criminal force, which remote observation does not fulfill.

cases.title: State of Delhi v. Rajiv Sharma
cases.facts:
Rajiv Sharma confronted a wealthy businessman, Mr. Gupta, in an isolated
underground parking lot. Rajiv held a switchblade to Mr. Gupta's throat
and demanded, "Transfer 5 Bitcoins to my wallet address right now, or I
will slit your throat." Terrified for his life, Mr. Gupta opened his
phone app and initiated the blockchain transfer of the cryptocurrency to
the provided address. Once the transfer was confirmed on the network
(which took about 10 minutes, during which Rajiv kept the knife at his
throat), Rajiv fled. He was caught a week later and charged with Robbery
(Section 390 IPC).
cases.issues:
- Can digital cryptocurrency (Bitcoin) be classified as "property"
capable of being the subject of Extortion or Robbery under the IPC?
- Is the act of forcing a digital transfer at knifepoint classified as
Extortion or does it escalate to the aggravated offense of Robbery?
- Does a digital transfer fulfill the requirement of "delivery of
property" in the presence of the offender?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The Prosecution argued for the higher charge of Robbery (Section 390).
They established that Bitcoin constitutes intangible movable property.
Robbery is an aggravated form of extortion. The State argued that Rajiv
intentionally put Mr. Gupta in instant fear of death, and in that very
presence and under that fear, induced Mr. Gupta to deliver the property
(the Bitcoins). The fact that the property moved through the blockchain
rather than physical hands is irrelevant; the extortion occurred in
physical presence with instant fear, fulfilling all ingredients of
Robbery.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Defense)
The Defense argued a highly pedantic reading of the IPC. They contended
that Robbery requires the physical "carrying away" of movable property
(like a watch or wallet). Since Bitcoin has no physical form, it cannot
be physically handed over or carried away. Therefore, the crime should,
at most, be Extortion (Section 383), which carries a significantly lower
penalty. Furthermore, they argued the "delivery" wasn't instantaneous;
the network took 10 minutes to confirm it, meaning the delivery happened
in cyberspace, not in Rajiv's physical presence.
cases.judgment:
The Sessions Court decisively convicted Rajiv Sharma of Robbery under
Section 392 of the IPC. The State prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court brilliantly adapted 19th-century penal statutes to 21st-century
digital realities. The judge ruled that "property" under the IPC includes
intangible assets that hold value. A digital transfer transfers ownership
and control, satisfying the legal requirement of "delivery." The Court
then explained the escalation from Extortion to Robbery. The crux of
Robbery (Section 390) is the immediacy of the threat and the presence of
the offender. Rajiv was physically present, holding a knife to the
victim's throat, inducing immediate terror, and forcing the immediate
execution of the transfer on the phone. The backend technical time taken
by the blockchain to confirm the transaction does not sever the immediacy
of the physical threat and the extortionate demand.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This is a landmark judgment bridging the gap between physical violence
and digital assets. It establishes that Cryptocurrency and digital
assets legally constitute "Property" under the IPC. Furthermore, it
sets the precedent that forcing digital transfers via immediate
physical threat constitutes Robbery (Section 390), not mere Extortion,
recognizing digital delivery as functionally equivalent to physical
handover.

cases.title: State of Karnataka v. Aryan
cases.facts:
Aryan, the lead software architect at a burgeoning legal-tech startup
named LexImperia, was fired after a bitter dispute with the board of
directors. A month later, LexImperia discovered that its proprietary
predictive-analysis algorithm had been copied and sold to a competitor.
The police investigated and alleged that Aryan had installed a logic bomb
and a backdoor in the company's servers prior to his termination. The
primary evidence was a series of system log files and email trails
downloaded from LexImperia's central servers by the investigating
officer onto a police hard drive. However, the police failed to secure a
certificate under Section 65B(4) of the Indian Evidence Act from the
system administrator at the time of seizure. Aryan was charged under
Sections 43 and 66 of the Information Technology Act and Section 379 of
the IPC (Theft).
cases.issues:
- Can electronic records (server logs and emails) be admitted as
secondary evidence in a criminal trial without a mandatory certificate
under Section 65B(4) of the Indian Evidence Act?
- Is the requirement of a Section 65B certificate procedural and curable,
or a mandatory condition precedent for admissibility?
- Can the theft of intangible digital source code constitute the offense
of "Theft" of movable property under Section 379 of the IPC?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State)
The Prosecution argued that the server logs unequivocally proved Aryan's
unauthorized access and data exfiltration. Relying on the Supreme Court's
earlier, more relaxed stance in Tomaso Bruno v. State of UP, the State
argued that Section 65B is not a complete code and that electronic
evidence can be proved under Sections 61 and 62 as well. They argued that
substantive justice should not be derailed by a mere procedural lapse
